hints: Look at the gradient of the velocity-time graph at point P - is it zero, positive or negative, and what does that say about acceleration?
Recall that $acceleration = resultant force / mass$, with weight acting down and air resistance acting up and increasing with velocity.
Since the sphere is still speeding up at P but the gradient is decreasing, compare the sizes of weight and air resistance needed for a downward but shrinking resultant force.
walkthrough: Identify from the graph that at point P the velocity is increasing because the curve is still rising, so the gradient and hence acceleration are positive downwards.
State the forces: constant downward weight and upward air resistance that grows as velocity grows.
Use Newton's second law: $F_{resultant} = weight - air resistance = m \times a$. A downward acceleration requires $weight > air resistance$.
Note that terminal velocity is only reached later when the gradient becomes zero and $weight = air resistance$, which has not happened at P.
Therefore the force diagram must show both arrows with the weight arrow longer than the air resistance arrow. This is option C.

options.A: Equal weight and air resistance would give zero resultant force and zero acceleration, but the gradient at P is still positive so velocity is still increasing.
options.B: At point P the velocity is non-zero so there must be an upward air resistance in air, not weight alone.
options.C: Downward weight is larger than upward air resistance, giving a net downward force and continued downward acceleration as shown by the positive gradient at P.
options.D: A larger upward air resistance than weight would give a net upward force and deceleration, but velocity is still increasing at P.
